nameStory: The ferruginous hawk gets its name from the Latin word 'ferruginous,' which means rust-colored or reddish-brown – perfectly describing the rich, rusty tones of its feathers. Its scientific name Buteo regalis literally means 'royal buzzard,' befitting this majestic bird that's the largest hawk in North America. Early naturalists also called it the 'ferrugineous rough-leg' because of its feathered legs that reminded them of the similar rough-legged hawk.
description: The ferruginous hawk is North America's largest hawk, a powerful bird of prey with broad wings built for soaring over open grasslands. These impressive raptors display beautiful rust-colored plumage on their backs and shoulders, with lighter underparts that can range from white to rufous. They're built like aerial battleships – heavy-bodied with long, broad wings that can span over four feet across. Unlike most hawks you'd see in New England forests, ferruginous hawks are birds of the wide-open western prairies and grasslands.

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Massive hawk with a heavy, robust body and exceptionally broad wings that dwarf other buteos – appears almost eagle-like in flight with slow, powerful wingbeats

idTips.label: Rust-colored Back
idTips.description: Rich, rusty-red or cinnamon-brown coloring on the back, shoulders, and wing coverts that catches sunlight with a warm, metallic sheen

idTips.label: Feathered Legs
idTips.description: Legs feathered all the way down to the toes, often with rufous or white plumage – gives a 'fuzzy boot' appearance when perched

idTips.label: Light Flight Feathers
idTips.description: Pale gray or whitish flight feathers with dark wingtips create a distinctive two-toned wing pattern visible from below during flight

idTips.label: Head Pattern
idTips.description: Large, broad head with a distinctive light-colored throat and darker crown, giving a somewhat owl-like facial appearance for a hawk

habitat: Ferruginous hawks are extremely rare visitors to New England, as they're birds of the western grasslands and prairies. On the handful of occasions they've been spotted here, it's typically been in large, open agricultural areas or coastal grasslands during migration or winter wandering. Any sighting in New England would be considered a major rarity worth reporting to birding communities.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen, but any spring sightings would likely occur during migration in March or April over large open areas or farm fields.
seasonality.summer: Virtually never present in New England during breeding season, as they nest exclusively in western North America's grassland habitats.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for a rare sighting during fall migration from September through November, when young birds may wander far from their normal range.
seasonality.winter: Occasional vagrant individuals might appear in winter, likely attracted to large agricultural areas with abundant rodent populations.

funFact: Despite being called a hawk, ferruginous hawks are so large and powerful that they can actually take down prey as big as jackrabbits and prairie dogs – some weighing nearly as much as the hawk itself – making them more like small eagles in their hunting abilities!
confusionNotes: In New England, the most likely confusion would be with a very large red-tailed hawk, but ferruginous hawks are noticeably bigger with much broader wings, feathered legs (red-tails have bare yellow legs), and more extensive rust coloring. Remember: if it looks almost too big to be a hawk and has 'fuzzy boots,' it might be this western rarity.
contextualKnowledge: The ferruginous hawk is considered the 'king of hawks' in western North America, but any sighting in New England should be carefully documented and reported, as there have been fewer than a dozen confirmed records in the region. Many reported sightings turn out to be large red-tailed hawks or other more common species.
compareHints: Ferruginous hawks absolutely dwarf their buteo relatives – they're significantly larger than red-tailed hawks with much broader wings and a more massive build. Unlike red-shouldered or broad-winged hawks that prefer forests, ferruginous hawks are strictly birds of open country. They share feathered legs with rough-legged hawks, but are much larger with more extensive rust coloring and a heavier build.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buteo hawks, red-tails are the largest and bulkiest, while red-shouldered hawks are more slender with distinctive reddish shoulder patches and prefer wooded areas.
Among buteo hawks in New England, red-shouldered hawks are the forest specialists with the most distinctive barring pattern.
Compared to its buteo relatives, the broad-winged hawk is the most forest-dependent and migratory.
Unlike the year-round resident Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Rough-legged Hawks are strictly winter visitors from the Arctic.
Compared to our common Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings and are built more for long-distance soaring.
